text: Best Phone Pouches That Block Wi-Fi and Cellular Signals Nov 9 Written by Brett Kleinberg Every signal-blocking pouch makes the same basic promise: put a phone inside, and calls, texts, notifications, and data stop reaching it. But the people buying these pouches want very different things from them. A traveler or privacy-minded owner wants a sleeve they control, one they can seal when it matters and open the moment it doesn’t. A school, testing center, or courthouse wants the opposite: hundreds of phones silenced at once, and confidence that none of them come out until someone in charge decides they should. This ranking is written mainly for institutions, with notes for individual buyers where their needs differ. We judged each of the five brands on how well it blocks signals and whether the maker has published testing to prove it, whether the pouch locks and who holds the key, what kind of support the company provides, and how it sells the product. Do You Need Signal Blocking, a Lock, or Both? Locking a phone away and blocking its signal solve two different problems. A locking pouch keeps the phone out of someone’s hands; a signal-blocking pouch keeps the phone itself silent and offline. Many phone-free schools need only the first. Once a student can’t reach their phone, it has already stopped being a distraction, whether or not it’s still receiving texts. Organizations that need signal blocking usually have a specific reason: An RFP, district policy, or exam rule requires it. Stored phones keep buzzing and chiming, and the noise is disrupting the room. Students are hotspotting a phone to a laptop, or screen mirroring, to reach sites the school network blocks. A court needs to keep jurors and witnesses from receiving outside messages or looking up information about the case during proceedings. The setting is an exam, a hearing, or a confidential meeting, where a connected device is a risk even when nobody is holding it. Airplane mode won’t cover these cases. For one thing, it relies on every single person turning it on and leaving it on. For another, NIST’s guidance on mobile device forensics notes that airplane mode doesn’t always shut off services such as GPS. A shielded pouch works the same way no matter how the phone is set, as long as it’s fully closed, since any gap in the closure lets signal through. A test of the finished pouch against a named standard tells a buyer more than a claim about the fabric. Closure and access control Whether the pouch locks, who can open it, and whether staff can tell if someone tried. With a roll-top or Velcro closure, that decision belongs to the person carrying it. Use at scale Whether the pouch is built and supported for hundreds of people at once, with unlocking equipment and a check-in routine. Implementation and program support What the vendor provides beyond hardware, such as policy help, training, launch support, and ongoing troubleshooting. Pricing model Whether the price is one-time or recurring, and what it includes beyond the pouch itself. Overall Ranking Ranked based on qualitative performance across the five criteria above. text: Yondr Phone-Free Program vs Off-and-Away Policy: What the Research Shows Oct 27 Written by Brett Kleinberg Two Policies That Start From the Same Rule Many schools have started their journey to a phone-free culture with a policy commonly referred to as off-and-away. Sometimes called away for the day, students switch their phones off and keep them out of sight in a backpack, a pocket, or a locker, and it's up to teachers to enforce the rule when a phone appears. Many other schools have started this same journey using a more proactive Yondr phone-free program. In a Yondr program each phone is locked in a pouch that the student carries, and it stays locked until dismissal. While both kinds of schools have the same sentence in the handbook, no phones during the school day, and the approach, enforcement and burden on teachers is quite different. In the largest national study of school phone restrictions to date, about 62 percent of schools have elected off-and-away as their first step into policy enforcement. What the Largest Study Found The study is a working paper that the National Bureau of Economic Research published in May 2026, written by economists at Stanford, Duke, the University of Pennsylvania, and the University of Michigan. It draws on data from more than 40,000 schools between 2019 and 2026 and compares schools that adopted Yondr with similar schools that didn't. Yondr supplied anonymized implementation data for it. Yondr did not fund the research, design the study, or review the findings before publication. The clearest findings in the paper were about phone use: Teachers reported that the share of students using phones in class for non-academic reasons fell from 61% to 13% in Yondr schools, an 80% reduction. Between classes, Yondr schools cut phone use by 53 percentage points, nearly three times the reduction achieved by off-and-away policies alone, according to Yondr's summary of the study . Teacher satisfaction with their school's phone policy went from about 26% to 75%. Within two years, students in Yondr schools reported well-being improvements approaching double those documented in major social media deactivation research, per the same summary. Why the Gap Opens Between Classes Off-and-away can do its best work in a classroom, when there's a teacher who is responsible for enforcement and they are willing to consistently address phones, even if it requires them to stop a lesson or activity to do so. Often, there is not the same kind of responsibility or oversight in the hallways, the lunchroom, or the bathrooms, and the rule gets thin there. Teachers themselves report: among high school teachers whose schools have a cellphone policy, 60% told Pew Research Center that it's difficult to enforce. A pouch moves enforcement to a single moment at the door and takes it off the teacher's desk for the rest of the day. Students still keep possession of their own phone; it isn't confiscated or collected, and it's never stored away from the student. Teachers are no longer asked to act as the phone police in every period. text: Phone-Free Testing Centers: Pouches vs Lockers for Exam Integrity Oct 27 Written by Brett Kleinberg Two Ways to Keep Phones Out of an Exam Testing centers bar phones from the exam room and have settled on two main ways of making sure. With lockers, the student powers the phone off and leaves it outside the testing room along with the coat and the backpack. With pouches, the phone is locked into a pouch at check-in and stays with the test-taker, sitting in view of the proctor, until check-out. The profession's own standards don't require either one. The National College Testing Association's standards ask for secure storage of examinee belongings and no access to them during testing, without saying it has to be a locker, though some exam sponsors do specify. LSAC tells LSAT candidates that their phones go in lockers provided at the test center. The Underlying Question: Where Is the Phone, and Who Can Reach It? Lockers put distance between the student and the phone. Iowa State University went this route in 2025, adding lockers, dividers, and cameras to two of its testing centers. Its testing manager told the Iowa State Daily that the lockers were meant to cut down on phone use and on the noise that bags and jackets make, and that misconduct reports had come down since they went in. The same article also describes the downsides. The renovation was paid for largely by a $630,000 award, and whether other centers get the same treatment depends on space and funding. One proctor described students locking their own ID inside the locker, and the line that builds outside the door while staff sort it out. A center that holds other people's property also has to say something about liability, which is why Arizona State's testing services , like many others, tell students they aren't responsible for items left in lockers. A pouch keeps the phone close and takes away the ability to open it. The phone stays with its owner for the whole exam, the owner can’t open the pouch until check-out, and the device sits on the desk where the proctor can see it. Many centers assign each pouch to a specific testing station or seat, which keeps inventory simple and makes any misuse easy to trace. How a Pouch Check-In Works Purdue Testing Services requires Yondr pouches for securing electronics and publishes its routine. At check-in the student puts their phone, smartwatch, and earbuds in a pouch, and a proctor locks it while they watch; the pouch then stays on the desk for the whole exam. For online exams that need two-factor authentication, the student logs in at their seat first and the phone goes into the pouch after that. At check-out, the pouch is unlocked at the desk. The Texas Board of Law Examiners applies the same model at a higher-stakes exam. It bars cell phones from the secure area of the bar exam unless they're secured in a Yondr pouch. text: How Tamper Evidence Works in School Phone Pouches Oct 27 Written by Brett Kleinberg When principals first ask about phone pouches, the question is almost always the same: can students break into them? Given enough time, a teenager can damage almost anything a school hands out, and that’s true of every pouch on the market. Perhaps the most practical question is whether staff can tell afterward that tampering has happened. Yondr pouches are durable and can withstand years of use under normal conditions, but are also built to be tamper-evident. If one has been opened, whether by accident or on purpose, staff can tell. This guide explains how the pouch does that, who is supposed to be able to open one under what circumstances, and how schools practically fit ppuch checks into an ordinary day. Tamper-Evident Does Not Mean Tamper-Proof The FDA drew this distinction in 1998, when it changed the wording of its packaging rules for over-the-counter medicines from "tamper-resistant" to "tamper-evident," on the grounds that the newer term better describes what packaging can actually do. The federal definition it adopted is still a good one: a tamper-evident package has "one or more indicators or barriers to entry which, if breached or missing, can reasonably be expected to provide visible evidence" that tampering has occurred. The same arrangement is behind evidence bags, ballot box seals, and the sealed packets that exam papers come in. All of them can be opened, but opening one leaves a mark, and somebody at the receiving end is responsible for noticing it. Who Can Open a Pouch A phone pouch is a form of access control. It sets out who can open it and under what circumstances: Students can't open it during the school day. Authorized staff can, at an unlocking base, at the times and places the school's policy allows. Anyone who forces it leaves evidence behind. Judged this way, a lock that resists for a long time and then gives way without a mark isn't much use to a school, since nobody learns anything from it. A pouch solution that shows an attempt has been made to hack it gives administrators of the policies something to actually follow up on. Access control doesn't mean taking the phone. Students keep possession of their own phone inside the locked Yondr pouch. Phones don’t need to be confiscated or collected, and it's never stored away from the student. How the Yondr Pouch Shows Evidence Yondr's pouch closes with a proprietary pushpin lock, patented in the US and built from metal and plastic components inside a durable outer. The current pouch uses a thicker pin and a stronger locking mechanism. Yondr doesn't describe it as unbreakable; the design goal is that deliberate damage is visible to staff. The lock is also integrated into the pouch rather than attached as a separate assembly. That distinction is worth asking any vendor about, because a lock attached as its own part introduces a seam, and a seam is where a closure can come away from a pouch without the lock itself being defeated. How Schools Use the Evidence Schools that run pouches well attach the checking to moments that already exist in the day, so nobody has a new inspection to run: At arrival. A damaged pouch is handled under the school's existing code of conduct, the same as any other conduct matter, and the pouch is replaced. text: How Phone-Free Events Work: Concerts, Comedy, Weddings and Launches Oct 27 Written by Brett Kleinberg A lot of people meet their first phone-free event at the door, when a staff member holds out a pouch and the line on the ticket suddenly makes sense. The questions that follow are practical ones: where the phone is going, whether you can get to it if the babysitter calls, and how long the line out of the building will be. Yondr's pouches have been used at more than 10,000 events around the world and have secured more than 20 million devices, and the routine that answers those questions has barely changed from an arena tour to a wedding for 150. This guide goes through it once, then looks at how it bends to fit concerts, comedy, weddings, and launches. The Routine, Door to Door Arrival. Each guest's phone goes into a Yondr pouch on the way in, and so do smartwatches. If your ticket lives on your phone, staff are there to open the pouch so it can be scanned. Inside. The pouch is locked once guests are in the phone-free area. From then on guests keep possession of their phone , which is never checked at a counter or collected by anyone. If someone needs their phone. Venues set up designated Phone Use Areas for this. A guest steps in, the pouch is opened, and it's locked again before they head back to their seat. Exit. A tap on an unlocking base opens the pouch. Bases and staff are placed at every exit, so the crowd leaves the way it normally would. How It Changes by Event Concerts and tours Yondr works with artists, venues, promoters, and labels on phone-free shows and tours, anything from arena runs and residencies down to listening parties and private studio sessions. At tour scale, most of the planning goes into flow: enough staff and unlocking bases at each door that several thousand people keep moving at a normal pace. Jack White has talked about what it's like from the stage: "People absolutely love it. You immediately know that they are engaged." Comedy Comedians go phone-free so they can try out new jokes, and so a tour's worth of material stays protected until the special. The same setup scales down to a club. The Comedy Store in Los Angeles has run every show device-free with Yondr since December 2024, with Phone Use Areas in the building. Weddings and private events At weddings, birthdays, and private parties the hosts are after presence and privacy more than leak prevention, and a phone-free ceremony keeps raised screens out of the aisle and out of the official photos. One couple described their wedding afterward: "We lived in the moment. No one was worried about their phone or posts on social media." Launches and brand events Product reveals, album playbacks, and premieres go phone-free so that the first images out are the ones the brand or the artist releases. Pinterest took the same approach at its 2026 Coachella space, which was phone-free, with visitors handed Yondr pouches on the way in, Marketing Brew reported . Film sets and tapings On film sets, live tapings, and stage productions the pouch protects work that hasn't been released yet and keeps cast and crew focused. In Yondr's event numbers for this year, sets account for more guests pouched than any other category. Yondr Events in 2026, by the Numbers Most phone-free events are a good deal smaller than a tour. text: Best Faraday Phone Pouches for Schools: Buyer's Guide Sep 23 Written by Brett Kleinberg A Faraday pouch is built around the promise to fully block the phone's signal, not just make it harder to reach. That promise is also the easiest one for a vendor to overstate, since "our fabric meets a shielding standard" and "our finished pouch was tested to block signal" sound identical in marketing copy but mean very different things for a classroom. This guide covers how to tell the difference and how the leading school-focused options compare. How to Evaluate a Faraday Claim Two different things get tested in this category, and only one of them tells a buyer what actually happens once a phone is inside the finished pouch a school will use every day. Weak disclosure: a vendor names a standard the shielding fabric meets and stops there. The material may perform well on a lab bench, but nothing confirms the finished product, with its seams, closure, and stitching, performs the same way. Strong disclosure: a vendor reports the fabric and the finished pouch separately, each tested against a named standard (IEEE 299-2006, MIL-STD 285, or NSA 94-106 are the common references) across a stated frequency range in decibels. Only strong disclosure tells a school what will actually happen in daily use, since a seam or a closure gap can leak signal even when the fabric itself is proven. Questions to Ask Before You Buy Was the fabric tested, the finished pouch, or both? Which standard was it tested against, and across what frequency range? Does the pouch also lock, or does it rely on the student to keep it closed? What happens for a student with a medical device that needs quick access? Is the price a one-time purchase or a recurring per-student fee, and what does it include beyond the pouch itself? text: Best Signal-Blocking Phone Pouches for Schools (2026) Sep 14 Written by Brett Kleinberg Schools and districts writing phone policies are increasingly identifying the need for a signal blocking by name, and the market is genuinely confusing. Some product provide signal interference without truly blocking all signals to the phone, but based on how these solutions are sold, most buyers cannot tell which solutions truly provide signal blocking properties from a spec sheet alone. Other signal blocking solutions do not actually provide for a locking mechanism to ensure the phone is secure and away. Does Your School Actually Need Signal Blocking? Signal blocking is not a requirement for a phone-free school. Well-run programs can create effective phone-free environments without it when implementation, training, and policy are right. A pouch that simply locks a phone away from a student for the day already removes the distraction; the phone doesn't need to be unreachable by radio for that to work. Schools that genuinely need signal blocking tend to have one of a few specific triggers: An RFP or district policy that requires it as a specification. Classes disrupted by notification sounds and vibration alerts even from a locked-away phone. Students hotspotting a phone to a laptop, or screen mirroring, to reach sites the school network blocks. If none of those apply to your building, a non-signal-blocking locking pouch, paired with the right rollout and policy, is likely to work as well and cost less to source. What New York Schools Must Do by Fall 2025 All public schools—including charters and BOCES—must enforce a Distraction-Free Schools policy starting Fall 2025. Approved options include lockers or secure locking systems like pouches. Ensure Communication Access Districts must establish and publish a way for parents/guardians to contact students during the day. Develop a Clear Enforcement Plan Must avoid suspensions and include: Demographic data reporting on violations An equity analysis A mitigation plan if disparities exist (Required beginning September 2026 ) Communicate the Policy Must be clearly posted online and available in the top 12 non-English languages spoken in the state upon request. title: The History of Cell Phone Policies in Schools: From Bans to the Phone-Free Movement
description: Former superintendent Dr. Peter Stiepleman outlines the shift from outright bans to structured phone-free environments—and why today’s school leaders must act to protect focus and well-being.
text: The History of Phones in Schools: How We Got Here and Where We’re Going Apr 23 Written by Guest User By Dr. Peter Stiepleman As a former school superintendent, I've been reflecting on the evolution of cell phones and cell phone policies in our schools, and it’s a journey that mirrors our changing relationship with technology. To understand how we got here - and where we need to go - it helps to look back. In the Beginning: A Straightforward Ban When cell phones first started showing up in schools, the response was relatively straightforward: ban them. The intention was to minimize disruptions and keep the focus on learning. However, this approach didn't consider the potential for technology as a learning tool. A Shift in Focus: Bring Your Own Device A shift began to occur around 2010 when educational leaders like Bill Daggett advocated for leveraging student-owned devices to enhance learning. At that time, schools primarily used computer labs and carts to include technology in the curriculum. Allowing students to bring their own phones, tablets, and laptops seemed like a practical way to expand digital access. Policies stipulated student devices could only be used for educational purposes with the intention of leveraging technology for learning, while still controlling its use. The Rise of Social Media and the Decline of Focus Unfortunately, as experts have retrospectively recounted, this coincided with the rapid rise of social media, which became a major part of our students' lives. The introduction of platforms like Instagram in 2010, and the integration of back-facing cameras in phones, made social media an essential part of students' daily routines. Features designed to be addictive, such as heart-shaped “likes,” notifications, and the ability to repost content created a strong pull for students, making it really difficult to stay focused on other things. Then came the pandemic. Remote learning further amplified this trend, as phones and social media became the primary window to the world for most people, especially children. Filters, avatars, and curated feeds created a constant pressure to perform, and a growing sense of isolation. When students returned to school in 2022, the impact was clear. Parents and educators noted a significant increase in concerns about phone usage and its impact on learning and well-being. One teacher documented over 1,300 notifications during a single class period, demonstrating the extent of the distraction. The mental health crisis among young people has become so acute that the former U.S. Surgeon General advocated for warning labels similar to those on alcohol and tobacco products to be associated with social media access. Research from experts like Jean Twenge and Jonathan Haidt , along with reports from Common Sense Media and Data & Society all point to the same conclusion: smartphones and social media are taking a toll on our kids. The Phone-Free Movement: A New Way Forward This brings us to the current movement toward phone-free schools, which differs significantly from a phone ban. Phone-free schools allow students to have their phones, but require they be put away during school hours - from bell to bell. It's not about taking phones away completely. title: Doomscrolling and Teenagers: Why It Happens and How to Help
description: Learn why teens are especially vulnerable to doomscrolling and how it impacts their mental health. Discover how phone-free spaces—like those created by Yondr—can help break the cycle and support student well-being.
text: Doomscrolling: Breaking the Cycle Apr 15 Written by Guest User Dr. David Franklin, Manager of Partner Programming In today’s digital world, people of all ages find themselves endlessly scrolling through negative news and distressing content. This habit, known as doomscrolling , keeps users engaged with an ongoing stream of alarming headlines and emotionally charged updates. But why are teenagers particularly vulnerable to this behavior, and what can be done to help them break free? To better understand the impact of doomscrolling on teens, let’s take a closer look at what it is, why it happens, and how it affects their well-being. What Is Doomscrolling? Doomscrolling is the act of consuming an ongoing flow of negative news, social media posts, and emotionally intense content. While staying informed is important, constant exposure to distressing material can overwhelm the mind, leading to heightened stress, anxiety, and a sense of helplessness. Why Do Teenagers Doomscroll? Teenagers are especially at risk. With social media being a central part of their lives, teens are encouraged to stay up-to-date on trending topics. Social media algorithms prioritize emotionally charged content, meaning the most sensational or negative stories end up on top of their feeds. The pressure to stay connected, coupled with easy access via smartphones, makes it easy for teens to fall into hours of scrolling. Because adolescents are more impressionable, repeated exposure to negative content can deeply affect their emotional well-being. The Negative Effects of Doomscrolling Doomscrolling doesn’t just distract—it has real mental and emotional consequences: Ways to Break the Cycle While it may seem difficult to break the doomscrolling habit, there are ways to reduce the impact of excessive screen time—and that’s where creating phone-free spaces, like the ones fostered by Yondr, can make a significant difference. Here’s how: Set Screen Time Limits: Implementing the Yondr Phone-Free Program in schools can help set natural boundaries for screen time. Yondr’s phone-free environment ensures students are not distracted by their devices during class, allowing them to focus more on learning and less on the negativity scrolling can bring. Shift Social Norms Around Phones: Removing the expectation to always be online allows students to build stronger, face-to-face connections. Phone-free learning environments foster a more positive and focused mindset for students. Encourage Digital Breaks: Encouraging regular breaks from screens can help teens reset and recharge. By using Yondr’s phone-free model, schools are helping students take these breaks, giving them time to engage in face-to-face interactions, mindfulness practices, and other activities that promote well-being. Promote Mindfulness and Hobbies: With fewer digital distractions, students can dive deeper into hobbies and creative outlets that help them cope with stress. Whether it’s a quiet moment to reflect or connecting with friends, breaking free from constant screen time allows teens to focus on what really matters. The Bottom Line Doomscrolling is a challenging habit to overcome, but creating phone-free spaces, both at home and in school, can make a big difference. Limiting screen time, encouraging positive offline engagement, and promoting healthier digital habits can help teens regain control and support their mental well-being. At Yondr, we’re committed to creating environments where students can focus on what truly matters—learning, connecting, and being present. By supporting phone-free schools, we’re helping to break the cycle of doomscrolling and promoting a more focused, balanced, and engaged educational experience. text: Key Themes from AASA 2025 Mar 31 Written by Guest User Dr. Peter Stiepleman, Yondr Senior Advisor We joined educators, administrators, and thought leaders from across the country at the AASA National Conference on Education 2025 in New Orleans to explore the evolving challenges and opportunities facing educators today. text: Banksy’s “Cut & Run” Exhibit Goes Phone‑Free with Yondr in Glasgow Aug 11 Written by Kate Reins How the world’s most famous street artist made his latest exhibit a distraction-free experience In a time when gallery-goers often spend more time capturing than contemplating, Banksy made a radical decision: no phones allowed. His 2023 solo exhibit, Cut & Run , at Glasgow’s Gallery of Modern Art (GoMA), was entirely phone-free —and powered by Yondr . Visitors locked away their phones in personal Yondr pouches at the entrance, trading selfies for stillness and screen-time for real-time. GoMA museum manager Gareth James explained the motivation simply: “The point is not to view the show through a phone, or the phone of someone standing in front of you, but to see it for yourself.” And visitors embraced it. Instead of facing a sea of screens, guests moved slowly, talked quietly, and immersed themselves in Banksy’s raw, political, and often deeply personal works. Inside Cut & Run The exhibit spanned 25 years of stencils , featuring original tools, design sketches, and behind-the-scenes elements from some of Banksy’s most iconic pieces: The Glastonbury stab vest worn by Stormzy The Sotheby’s shredder , used to destroy Girl with Balloon mid-auction A recreated prison cell , inspired by Banksy’s mural on Reading Gaol A pillow-fight mural originally painted on the West Bank barrier wall Banksy himself revealed a rare personal note in the exhibit's opening statement: “I’ve kept these stencils hidden away for years, mindful they could be used as evidence in a charge of criminal damage... But that moment seems to have passed.” The Impact Was Immediate 180,000+ visitors over 10 weeks — making it GoMA’s most attended show ever Extended overnight hours to meet demand, with doors open until 5 AM on weekends Phones locked, but guests could take home a staff-shot Polaroid as a keepsake The phone-free policy didn’t deter anyone—in fact, it enhanced the experience. Attendees described it as “intimate,” “more human,” and “unlike any gallery they’d been to before.” Why Banksy Chose Yondr Yondr creates spaces to be here now —whether in classrooms, courtrooms, concerts, or cultural spaces. By choosing Yondr, Banksy ensured: Zero distractions or unauthorized photos Complete focus on the art A shared, screen-free atmosphere for reflection In a world where most exhibits go viral before they even open, Banksy flipped the script—letting the experience speak for itself. title: Frequently Asked Questions
text: FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS What Is Yondr? Yondr creates phone-free spaces for artists, comedians, teachers, organizations, and more. The Yondr system is a simple solution that allows you to maintain possession of your phone at all times. What Is A Phone-Free School? A phone-free school is a distraction-free learning environment where students keep their smartphones and other personal technology (airpods/apple watches) in Yondr pouches from arrival to dismissal. Yondr works with thousands of schools across 27 countries and all 50 U.S. States. What Is A Phone-Free Show? At a phone-free show, artists and audiences can enjoy the performance in the moment and without distraction, creating a better experience for everyone. No cell phones, smart watches, cameras, or recording devices are permitted in the performance area. How Does It Work? Upon arrival at the venue, all phones and smart watches are placed in Yondr pouches by our staff. Guests maintain possession of their phones at all times. Anyone may access their phone during the show by entering one of the designated Phone Use Areas located throughout the venue. When the show is over, guests can unlock their Yondr pouches at any exit. LEARN MORE → Do I Maintain Possession Of My Phone At All Times? Yes. You will maintain possession of your phone and are responsible for it throughout the duration of the event. Will The Pouch Affect My Phone In Any Way? No My ticket is on my phone. What do I do? It’s preferable to have a hard ticket for entry, but Yondr staff will be standing by to unlock your phone so you can access your mobile ticket in order to enter the venue. I have a babysitter at home — Where can I check my phone? I am on-call for work — Where can I check my phone? Set your phone to vibrate as you enter the venue. You’ll be able to feel your phone vibrate through the Yondr pouch when you receive calls or texts. You may use your phone at any time throughout the event at designated Phone Use Areas inside the venue. What is a Phone Use Area? Guests are able to use their phones at designated Phone Use Areas inside the venue. All phones must be secured in Yondr pouches before guests re-enter the performance space. How do I unlock my phone after the show? Yondr staff will be stationed at all exits to unlock your phone at the end of the show. After Yondr staff unlocks your pouch, simply remove your items and toss the pouch in one of the bins stationed at exit points. Does it take long to unlock the Pouch and leave the venue? No. Yondr staff are located at each exit to quickly unlock your pouch. We find that leaving a phone-free show is usually faster. It’s amazing how quickly people move when they aren’t busy screen-touching. I didn’t know about the phone policy. What if I don’t want to do this? This is the show policy, and as a result we cannot allow entry to any guests with cell phones or smart watches if they are not secured in a Yondr pouch. What happens if there is an emergency in the venue and I can’t access my phone? All venue staff and security have cell phones and radios. Should an emergency occur, they are trained to implement and execute safety and emergency procedures. Guests should follow all venue instructions and evacuate immediately in the case of an emergency. Yondr Venue Staff will have hand-held unlocking devices outside at a safe distance from the venue. If I lose something at a Yondr show, who do I contact? Before contacting us, please check with the venue of the show/event, as any items found the night of are left with the venue’s customer service department. title: FAQ
text: FAQ If I have Yondr staff at my event, what time do they arrive? We recommend having staff arrive 1 hour or 45 minutes before guests arrive. Our setup only takes around 15 minutes. This will give them plenty of time to touch base with security and the event team before people arrive to be pouched. Does Yondr require power or electricity to lock and unlock? Yondr equipment does not require any power or electricity. How do I return the equipment? If your Yondr equipment was shipped to you, you can find the return shipping labels in the original box. Please place the labels on the original box and drop it off at your local FedEx. If you cannot locate the labels, please email your sales lead. If your equipment was dropped off by a staff member, your sales lead will be in touch regarding an in person pick up. What happens if I can’t find my return shipping labels? You can email your sales lead who will provide you with a return shipping label. If my event has metal detectors, should Yondr be stationed before or after them? Yondr should be stationed before the metal detectors. This way any hidden devices can be detected that were not offered up to be pouched. Do you provide metal detectors? We do not provide metal detectors or any other security equipment. We only provide the equipment needed to lock and unlock phones in pouches. What do I need to set up Yondr? Other than the equipment we provide, all you need is a table and chairs to be set up as close to the entrance of the phone free space as possible. No power or electricity is needed. What equipment should I expect to receive? Pouches, unlocking bases and tote bags to hold the pouches. If you have a capacity of over 210, you will also receive hampers that the totes fit into. Hampers can also be utilized for patrons/ guests to drop their pouch in on their way out. Please make sure to check that all of your equipment arrived as soon as you receive your shipment. What do we tell guests who request to keep their phone because of a babysitter or because they are on call for work? We suggest guests place their phones on vibrate so they can feel it when notified. They can then have their pouch unlocked to use outside of the phone free space. How far in advance do I need to confirm Yondr in order to ship the equipment to me in time? We ask for you to confirm 3 weeks before your event in order for equipment to arrive on time. Are magnets used in Yondr unlocking bases? Yes. This product uses magnets as part of its unlocking mechanism. Do Yondr unlocking bases interfere with implanted medical devices? Yondr does not provide medical advice regarding use with implanted medical devices. Magnets may interfere with certain medical devices such as shunts or cardiac devices. For users with medical shunts or other devices, please consult with a medical professional or refer to medical device manufacturer’s guidance on safe distance. Do all Yondr pouches require the use of a magnetic unlocking base? No. Some Yondr pouches do not require the use of a magnetic unlocking base. Yondr's product range also includes a velcro pouch, which can be opened directly by the user, without any additional unlocking equipment.

text: BE HERE NOW: A PHONE-FREE HOMECOMING EVERYONE WILL REMEMBER Homecoming is one of the best nights of the school year: a chance to dress up, dance with friends, and make memories students will actually want to remember. But here’s the thing: if everyone’s glued to their phones, it’s way too easy for them to miss the magic happening right in front of them. A phone-free homecoming doesn’t mean less fun. It means more . More dancing, more laughter, and more moments that feel real instead of staged. Here are some creative ways to keep the night memorable for students without needing a single phone screen: 1. Photo Booths and Polaroids You don’t need different apps or filters to get a great picture. Imagine students stepping into a photo booth decked out with crazy props like oversized glasses, feather boas, cowboy hats, and backdrops in your school colors. Add a Polaroid or instant-print camera and suddenly you’ve got a memory they can actually hold in their hands as they leave for the night. The best part? These photos aren’t meant to be perfect. They’re funny, messy, and one of a kind, just like the night itself. Students can trade them with friends, tape them up in their lockers, or post them on their walls at home. This is a much better way for students to remember the evening than scrolling through 100 blurry selfies the next day. 2. Memory Wall Think of this as Instagram, but offline. A giant wall covered in colorful sticky notes, doodles, and Polaroid snapshots where everyone adds their own piece of the night. Students can write down their favorite dance floor moment, leave an inside joke for their best friend, or post that goofy Polaroid they just took in the photo booth. By the end of the night, the wall tells the story of homecoming in real time. And the coolest part? Everyone’s included. No likes, no followers, just memories anyone can literally walk up to and touch. Instead of students worrying about who’s going to “like” a post, students get to be part of something real. On a memory wall, every note and picture matters the same. No algorithms, no pressure, no popularity contest. It’s not about who gets the most attention. It’s about creating one giant highlight reel together. And unlike a post that disappears in 24 hours, the wall can live on in your school as a reminder of the night for everyone to see. 3. Yearbook-Style Guestbook Imagine a giant blank book at the entrance where everyone writes shout-outs, doodles, or leaves their “Homecoming 2025 was the BEST!” stamp. Students can use markers, glitter pens, and stickers to make their shout-out stand out. Think of this as their own mini yearbook just for that one night. When students flip through it later, they won’t just remember the dance. They’ll remember their friends who made it fun. 4. Postcards to the Future This one’s a little like time traveling. Students will grab a blank postcard and write a quick note to their future self: “Remember when the DJ played that one song and the whole room went crazy?” or “This was the night we laughed until we cried.” Students will turn their postcards into a special mailbox before they leave the dance. Months later, school officials will mail every postcard back to the students. By then, students will have forgotten what they wrote, or even that they created the postcard in the first place, making it even more fun. It’s like getting a memory straight out of the past, delivered right to your physical mailbox. A phone-free homecoming is more than a trend. It’s an opportunity to foster genuine connection, presence, and community among students.
